lede: Futures flat after Friday's Nasdaq 100 record; no Iran deal, but oil holds near $102; Nikkei tops 70,000.

single_name_moves.venue: Paris, after agreeing to buy PTC (Reuters)

geo_headlines: FUTURES ARE FLAT AFTER FRIDAY'S NASDAQ 100 RECORD. S&P 500 futures are 7,770.50 (-0.09%) and Nasdaq 100 futures 31,021.25 (-0.13%) as of 6:59 AM ET. Friday the Nasdaq 100 closed at 30,807.93, above its September 22 record; the S&P 500 closed at 7,722.72, 0.98% below its August 13 record.

OIL IS PULLED BOTH WAYS. Brent December is $102.69 (+0.4%) and WTI November $90.52 (-0.6%). Brent fell to $101.59 early as Middle East exports recovered and the G7 reserve release took hold (Independent). It firmed after Yemen's Houthis said they launched missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and Khurais (Reuters). **OPEC+ kept November output targets steady on Sunday; its core members are still pumping about 5 million barrels a day below prewar levels (Reuters).**

IRAN: NO DEAL OVER THE WEEKEND. Parliament speaker Qalibaf said Sunday the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven conditions from the June interim agreement are met; Foreign Minister Araghchi said Iran's plan could reopen it within seven days if accepted (Reuters). Trump said Saturday Iran faces "the easy way or the hard way" (Iran International).

ASIA ROSE; THE NIKKEI TOPPED 70,000. The Nikkei jumped 2.5% in morning trading to 70,037.61, its first time above 70,000 in three months; Hong Kong was unchanged and Australia rose 0.1% (AP). Mainland China and South Korea were closed for holidays.

FRANCE IS WEIGHING ON THE EURO. The euro hit a 17-month low on French fiscal worries and political uncertainty (Bloomberg, via investingLive); EUR/JPY is 176.88 (-0.6%). France's CAC 40 fell 0.9%, with Schneider Electric down 9.1% after agreeing to buy PTC (Reuters). Germany's DAX and the FTSE 100 opened slightly higher (QNA).

YIELDS EASED OVERNIGHT. The 10-year was 5.26% and the 2-year 4.81% in Asian trading (Reuters), after Friday's Treasury closes of 5.28% and 4.83%. FedWatch still shows a 21.0% chance of an October hike and 85.0% for December, as of Friday's CME close. Gold is $4,191.50 (+0.7%).

TODAY: SERVICES DATA. S&P Global services PMI final at 9:45 and ISM services at 10:00 (August 55.4). This week: FOMC minutes Wednesday at 2:00 PM, jobless claims Thursday, Michigan sentiment Friday; Constellation Brands Tuesday, PepsiCo Thursday, Delta Friday (CNBC calendar).
client_frame_short: Markets start the week calm. Futures are flat after the Nasdaq 100 closed at a record on Friday, and Asian stocks rose, with Japan's Nikkei above 70,000. **The weekend brought no deal with Iran, but oil is holding near $102 because Gulf exports are recovering and governments are releasing reserves.** Treasury yields eased a little overnight, and an October Fed hike now looks unlikely after Friday's weak jobs report. For clients, nothing here calls for changes; the tests this week are the services data this morning and the Fed minutes on Wednesday.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the story is a quiet start after a big week.

Where we are: Friday's jobs report showed just 29,000 jobs added in September, and unemployment rose to 4.2%. Markets read that as a cooling economy, which takes pressure off the Fed. The odds of an October rate hike fell to about one in five. The Nasdaq 100 closed at a record. The S&P 500 is within 1% of its August record.

The weekend: Iran said the Strait of Hormuz stays closed until its conditions are met, and President Trump said he has a decision to make. That sounds alarming, but oil barely moved. Gulf exports have been recovering toward prewar levels, the G7 is releasing 100 million barrels of reserves, and OPEC+ left its targets unchanged. Brent is about $102.70, up less than half a percent from Friday.

The bond market: the 10-year Treasury yield is about 5.26%, just below Friday's close. Long-term rates remain the main pressure point for clients, mortgages and valuations. They stayed high even after a weak jobs report, because inflation and heavy government borrowing drive them more than hiring does.

Overseas: Japan's stock market topped 70,000 for the first time since July. In Europe, worries about France's budget pushed the euro to its lowest level in 17 months, a reminder that high government debt is a global theme, not just an American one.

This week: the services surveys this morning show whether the slowdown is spreading beyond hiring. The Fed minutes on Wednesday show how many officials wanted to keep raising rates.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds now pay about 5% for a decade, an opportunity to lock in income, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40%, a 30-year above 5.75%, or a resumption of US strikes on Iran that sends Brent well above $105.
